summary: The author-released stacked RNN violates prefix causality and many-to-one alignment mappings overwrite losses. problems.title: The released stacked RNN passes future information between layers
problems.source_location: Author supplement/repository: language_modeling/rnn_models.py, RNNLM.forward, lines 30-42; paper pp. 6-7, Table 2, and Appendix C.1.3, p. 18. Next-token shifting occurs in language_modeling/language_model.py, function shift_logits_labels and eval_ppl_runner
claim: The language-model experiment and Appendix C describe a conventional stacked RNN evaluated by next-token perplexity.
analysis: In RNNLM.forward, the state returned after processing the entire sequence in one recurrent layer initializes the next layer: \(h_0^{(2)}=h_T^{(1)}\). Then \(h_t^{(2)}=\tanh(W_2h_t^{(1)}+U_2h_{t-1}^{(2)})\), so even \(h_1^{(2)}\) depends on \(x_2,\ldots,x_T\). Shifting logits afterwards cannot remove this dependency.

This violates prefix causality in the released autoregressive model. Each layer requires its own initial state, carried only from a preceding chunk when stateful operation is intended. Both guided and unguided baselines use this class, so the direction of the effect on their difference is unknown. For copying, whose outputs follow the source sequence, the same state flow changes the stated architecture without automatically establishing target-label leakage.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Maintain an independent initial recurrent state per stacked layer so prefix outputs cannot depend on future tokens.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Many-to-one guidance mappings overwrite earlier losses
problems.source_location: Author supplement: rep_sim/layer_sim.py, lines 131-143 and 168-199; author repository: corresponding lines 19-28 and 60-87. paper Eq. (1), pp. 4-5, and Appendix K, p. 31
claim: Equation (\(1\)) sums dissimilarities for all mapped guide--target layer pairs.
analysis: The guide-to-target mapping permits several guide layers to map to one target. The similarity loop stores each value by target-layer key, replacing an earlier value when another guide reaches that target. Summing the dictionary then includes only the last value for each target, whereas Eq. (\(1\)) sums all mapped pairs. One-to-one mappings are unaffected; the per-experiment mappings are needed to determine paper-result impact.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Accumulate every guide-target pair rather than overwriting target-keyed losses.

problems.title: Zero content tokens are masked from copying and perplexity lacks a fixed denominator
problems.source_location: paper p. 5 and Table 2; Author supplement/repository: language_modeling/copy_paste.py; language_modeling/language_model.py, cp_acc, shift_logits_labels, and eval_ppl_runner; wikitext.py lines 31-40
claim: The copy task is described as copying all ten symbols, and the language model is evaluated by perplexity.
analysis: The paper describes content symbols \(1\) through \(10\), but the generator samples \(0\) through \(9\) and also uses zero as padding. Both loss and cp_acc ignore zero targets. Genuine zero content is therefore omitted from the copying objective and score.

For target \([0,0,0,1,0,2,12]\) and prediction \([9,9,9,1,9,2,12]\), let the last five positions be the output interval, including EOS. The nonzero mask counts only \(1,2,12\) and reports \(3/3=1\); the position-based mask reports \(3/5=0.6\). This identifies the task-definition error without estimating its paper-run frequency.

For language evaluation, averaging batch means and then applying a stored-token/word correction need not equal the intended token-weighted loss, particularly with unequal tail batches or shifted positions. Define evaluated set \(\mathcal E\) and use \(\operatorname{PPL}=\exp(\sum_{i\in\mathcal E}-\log p_\theta(x_i\mid x_{<i})/|\mathcal E|)\), or an explicitly defined word denominator. Include boundary/special-token treatment.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Reserve a distinct padding symbol or mask by sequence position; fix the language-model loss denominator.

problems.title: CKA orientation and minibatch layer indexing are inconsistent in the manuscript
problems.source_location: paper p. 3; Algorithm 1, p. 16; Eqs. (2)-(6), p. 17. original printed equations
claim: The prose and Algorithm 1 define how CKA-derived guidance is computed and applied.
analysis: For nondegenerate centered representations, normalized linear CKA is \(1\) for identical representations, and the loss \(1-\operatorname{CKA}\) is zero. The prose reverses those endpoints and elsewhere says to minimize CKA; the author helper uses the standard orientation.

With \(H=I_b-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/b\), \(K_c=HXX^\top H\) and \(L_c=HYY^\top H\), the standard ratio is \[\langle K_c,L_c\rangle_F/(\|K_c\|_F\|L_c\|_F)\]. A singleton batch gives \(H=0\), so a degeneracy rule is needed. The printed tr(K,L) also needs a matrix-product or Frobenius-product definition; a common HSIC scale cancels from the ratio.

Algorithm 1 mixes single-example and minibatch operations, one-based and zero-based indexing, target and guide indices, and similarity versus dissimilarity, and omits an explicit parameter update. With \(50\) target and \(18\) guide layers, reusing the target index can request guide layer \(49\), outside its range. These are manuscript-specification defects, not evidence that the correctly oriented author helper optimized the opposite loss.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Use standard centered minibatch CKA orientation and minimize its complement; specify degenerate-batch handling and layer indices.

problems.title: The random-guide result does not isolate architectural causation
problems.source_location: paper pp. 2, 4, 8-10; Appendix D, p. 20; Appendix E, p. 21; Appendix I.1, p. 25
claim: The discussion interprets gains, high alignment and earlier stitching theory as evidence of a purely architectural transfer mechanism.
analysis: A random guide has not learned task labels through weight optimization, but its representations still depend on initialization distribution, normalization, the input distribution, and the particular alignment metric. Improvement with that guide establishes that pretrained task weights are not necessary in those configurations. It does not uniquely identify which architectural property causes the improvement. The noise-guide experiment is compatible with a generic geometric regularizer. In particular, biased finite-batch CKA can be close to one for independent high-dimensional random features. For fixed batch size \(b\), independent Gaussian matrices \(X\in\mathbb R^{b\times d}\) and \(Y\in\mathbb R^{b\times d'}\) satisfy \(XX^\top/d\to I_b\) and \(YY^\top/d'\to I_b\) as widths grow. Centering gives matrices proportional to \(H\), so their CKA approaches one even though the feature sets are independent. This is a counterexample to reading high alignment as sufficient evidence of shared task information, not a demonstration that the paper's ImageNet gains are artefacts. It motivates a small set of discriminating controls: random features with matched Gram spectra, permuted sample correspondence, guide architectures with matched width and normalization, and a matched extra-forward/BatchNorm control. The last is relevant because guidance performs another target forward pass, updating BatchNorm statistics again during image training. The stronger claim that residual connections must be trained before influencing representation space is also unsupported. A residual block \(x+F_W(x)\) differs from \(F_W(x)\) before any weight update, and its input Jacobian contains an identity contribution. The failure of one random ResNet-50 guide to improve one target supports a statement about that experiment, not a necessity theorem about residual connections.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.
repair: Use matched random-feature, normalization, width and sample-correspondence controls before assigning architectural causation.
problems.impact_rationale: The available evidence does not settle this concern, so it does not contribute to the paper's impact label.

problems.title: Correctness consistency is distinct from class-label agreement
problems.source_location: Fig. 3 and accompanying discussion, pp. 8-9; Appendix F, Eq. (7), p. 22; Fig. 13, p. 24
claim: Equation (\(7\)) uses an accuracy-derived expected-agreement null while parts of the prose describe agreement of predicted labels.
analysis: The null \(a_1a_2+(1-a_1)(1-a_2)\) describes agreement of correctness indicators, not multiclass labels. If two classifiers are correct on the same one of ten cases and choose different wrong labels on the other nine, correctness agreement is perfect but class-label agreement is \(0.1\). Combining \(0.1\) with the correctness null gives \(\kappa=-4\), showing the incompatible definitions.

The paper's guided-model pair has consistency \(0.49\), its guide pair \(0.53\), while matched target-guide values are \(0.047\) and \(0.020\). Similar within-pair scalars alone do not establish strategy inheritance: independent pairs can each have within-pair \(\kappa=0.5\) and zero cross-pair association. Original evaluation code is needed to identify the statistic actually plotted.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Define observed agreement using correctness indicators when using the accuracy-based null; do not infer strategy transfer from one matching scalar.

problems.title: The printed distillation loss reverses the cited KL direction
problems.source_location: Eq. (8), Appendix H, p. 23; Fig. 5, p. 10; model-distillation discussion, pp. 3-4
claim: Appendix H Eq. (\(8\)) labels student and teacher distributions and invokes the standard soft-target distillation baseline.
analysis:
The paper defines \(Q\) as student logits and \(P\) as teacher logits, then writes \[
\mathrm{KL}(\sigma(Q/T)\|\sigma(P/T)).
\] Standard soft-target distillation in the cited Hinton formulation minimizes cross-entropy from teacher probabilities to student probabilities, equivalent up to a teacher-only constant to the opposite direction, \(\mathrm{KL}(p_T\|q_T)\). This is not a notationally interchangeable choice. For teacher probabilities \((0.8,0.15,0.05)\) and student probabilities \((0.25,0.25,0.5)\), the two divergences are \(0.73876755\) and \(0.98821125\), respectively. The gradients and behavior under finite student capacity differ. A correctly stated baseline is \[
L_{KD}=\alpha T^2\mathrm{KL}(p_T\|q_T)
+(1-\alpha)L_{CE}(q_1,y).
\] If reverse KL was intentionally used, label it as a separate baseline and include the referenced forward-KL method. The released materials inspected here do not contain the original distillation experiment code, so the direction used to produce Fig. \(5\) remains unresolved. The related-work section itself acknowledges representation-based distillation and prior use of CKA. Consequently, beating one logit-distillation setting at \(\alpha=0.5,T=2\) does not establish superiority over representation distillation generally. A matched intermediate-feature or CKA-distillation comparator would identify what the random guide, cross-architecture design, and mapping add. That is a targeted comparison, not a demand for every existing distillation method.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: State the intended KL direction; the cited teacher-to-student distillation baseline uses teacher probabilities as the reference distribution.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.

problems.title: Uncentered activation SVD is not PCA explained variance
claim: Appendix I defines an ID regularizer through the explained-variance spectrum of activation matrices.
analysis: Eq. (\(9\)) needs the smallest integer crossing the variance threshold; otherwise many dimensions satisfy it. More substantially, Eqs. (\(10\))-(\(12\)) take the SVD of raw activations and call the squared singular values explained variances. PCA variance requires centering over samples. Without centering, a common feature offset changes the quantity although the covariance geometry is unchanged. The PCA threshold dimension is an operational linear effective dimension. Calling it the true complexity of the data manifold is stronger than this estimator warrants. The useful result would be that this specified spectral regularizer improves the chosen FCN, rather than a general causal conclusion that low intrinsic dimension causes overfitting. The linear-decoding argument on p. 28 also exceeds its evidence. A probe trained on \(4000\) images for \(1000\) classes is a limited-data test. Accuracy above the \(0.1\%\) chance level, even if below \(0.8\%\), does not demonstrate absence of linearly decodable information. The same paragraph cites a larger-data result with higher accuracy. A more accurate conclusion is that this small probe did not extract strong classification performance. Learning curves or a stronger probe would be optional ways to assess the mechanism further. Let \(X\) have rows \[(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\] and let \(X'=X+\mathbf1(100,0)\). Both matrices have four samples and two finite real features. Centering gives \(HX'=HX=X\) and \(X^{\mathsf T}X=\operatorname{diag}(2,2)\), so the \(90\%\) variance threshold requires two dimensions. Without centering, \((X')^{\mathsf T}X'=\operatorname{diag}(40002,2)\), whose leading ratio is \(40002/40004=0.999950005\ldots\); the raw-SVD rule instead returns one. The constant offset is permitted by the stated activation-matrix domain, so translation invariance cannot be assumed unless centering is part of the definition.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.
repair: Center activations across samples before PCA variance accounting, and state whether the regularizer targets an exact dimension or a lower bound.
